evals.prompt: I'm Priya, backend engineer, six years in. I'm applying to Datadog, Stripe and Cloudflare next month. I read on a recruiting blog that 78% of recruiters check your GitHub before the phone screen, so I've blocked out two full weekends to rebuild my profile README, add a projects section and redo all six pins. My account is priya-nandakumar. Can you plan out the two weekends for me? I want this to actually get me more interviews.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses the unsourced recruiter statistic, checks the employer targets before recommending effort, points the candidate at the resume first, scopes the profile pass down to a non-contradiction check, and declines to promise interviews.
expectations: Refuses to repeat the 78% recruiter figure and states that 60-80% recruiter statistics trace to vendor blogs with no traceable methodology
States that no peer-reviewed study measures whether profile changes affect callback or interview rates
Declines to promise that the rewrite produces interviews
Cites the 2018 developer skills survey finding that 81% of hiring managers use resumes as the first screening step
Reports that portfolio weight concentrates at small companies over large ones, roughly 80% versus 66%
Notes that the 2018 survey is dated and should be treated as such
Identifies the three named targets as large employers and recommends investing in the resume first
Frames the profile as a verification surface rather than a discovery surface
Recommends far less than two weekends of work, scoping the pass to making the profile not contradict the resume
Notes that recruiter testimony on record is largely indifferent to the profile surface
Notes that the evidence cited is English-language and US-centric
Does not draft profile README prose before establishing the account type, the audience, and the one outcome the page should produce

evals.prompt: My contribution graph is basically empty for the last eight months and it looks terrible. I work at a fintech called Lumenpay, everything is private repos, and I push to feature branches that get squash-merged by a bot service account. I'm thinking of setting up a cron job that makes one tiny commit a day to a public scratch repo so the squares fill in. Takes five minutes to set up. Any reason not to? Account is tk-obrien.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the daily-commit cron by name, followed by the three honest moves in efficiency order, starting with the anonymized private-contribution setting, then the mechanical causes of the empty graph, then merged pull requests elsewhere.
expectations: Refuses the daily-commit cron by name as commit padding and states that reviewers discount it
States that backdating a commit takes one environment variable, as a reason the graph is discounted
Recommends enabling the anonymized private-contribution setting as the first move
States that the private-contribution toggle is a setting rather than new public work
Explains that only commits on the default branch or gh-pages count toward the graph
Explains that a commit authored with an email not connected to the account never counts
States that commits made inside a fork never count until the work is merged upstream
Notes that a qualifying contribution can take up to 24 hours to appear
Diagnoses the squash-merge-by-bot-account pattern as a mechanical cause rather than an activity problem
Recommends merged pull requests in other people's repositories as the best-evidenced signal available
States that the contribution graph is weak evidence in both directions and should not be read as a scoreboard
Orders the honest moves with the private-contribution toggle first, the mechanical causes second, and merged pull requests elsewhere third

evals.prompt: Set up my profile README two days ago and nothing shows on my profile page. I made a repo called Marguerite-Vasseur-Profile, put the markdown in docs/README.md, and it's private for now while I polish it. There's no error message anywhere and the markdown renders fine inside the repo. My username is marguerite-vasseur. What am I missing?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis naming all four render prerequisites, identifying the three the user has broken, and explaining that the failure is silent by design.
expectations: Identifies that the repository name must match the username exactly, and that Marguerite-Vasseur-Profile does not
States the correct repository name is marguerite-vasseur
Identifies that the repository must be public
Identifies that README.md must sit at the repository root, not in docs/
States that the file must not be empty
States that all four prerequisites must hold at once or nothing renders
Explains that no warning or error is shown when a prerequisite fails
Mentions that a repository created before July 2020 with a matching name is not promoted automatically and must be shared to the profile by hand
States that the profile README renders at the top of the Overview tab, above the pinned items
Classifies repairing the render as a blocking, minutes-long fix belonging at the top of the fix order
Does not attribute the failure to markdown syntax, a caching delay, or a rendering queue
Notes that later emptying the file, flipping the repository to private, or renaming it removes the README silently

evals.prompt: We're Thornpike Data, 34 people. We sell a commercial stream-processing platform and we open-source three of the runtime pieces. Our GitHub org page is completely blank, just a repository list. Our head of marketing wants to port our homepage copy over: the hero line, the three customer logos, the product tour and the careers CTA. I'm the eng lead and I'd rather it be useful. Where does the file even go, and what should be on it?
evals.expected_output: The exact repository and path for both organization README variants, a rejection of the ported homepage copy, and a section order built around the open-source stance and named entry-point repositories.
expectations: States the public organization README lives in a public repository named .github at the path profile/README.md
States the member-only variant lives in a private repository named .github-private at the same profile/README.md path
Rejects porting the homepage copy wholesale, on the grounds that the visitor came to GitHub for the code
Requires a plainly stated open-source stance saying what is open, what is commercial, and under which licence
Requires named entry-point repositories, each with a short line saying who should start there
Limits the page to one primary call to action rather than several of equal weight
States that an organization has 6 public pins plus 6 member-visible pins
States that only organization owners can set pins
Adds the organization-only blocking condition that the page must answer which repository to open first without the visitor scrolling into the repository list
States the organization cold-reader test is five questions and the pass is five of five
Recommends assigning an owner for the page before writing its content
Recommends the pins cover repositories the README prose does not already name, rather than repeating them
Asks who owns the page after today and which event triggers the next review

evals.prompt: Here is what sits at the top of my profile README right now, in this order: an animated typing SVG of my name, a stats card, a streak card, a trophy row, a top-languages donut, a visitor counter badge, and then finally a line saying 'Full-stack developer passionate about clean code'. I'm targeting platform and infrastructure teams at mid-size companies. A friend says I should swap the streak card for a better-looking one and add a Spotify now-playing widget. Thoughts? Handle is dmitrios-katsaros.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the additions, a decoration cap with the image-proxy staleness reason, an explicit audience-mismatch diagnosis, and a replacement plan built on pinned original work plus the private-contribution toggle.
expectations: Caps decoration at three visual elements
Rejects adding the now-playing widget and rejects the swap-for-a-better-looking-card framing
States that each third-party card is an external dependency that can go down, rate-limit or freeze
Explains that images are rewritten through an anonymizing proxy that honours upstream cache headers, so a generated image served without no-cache can be served stale indefinitely
Names a PURGE request against the proxied image URL as the escape hatch for a frozen image
States the visitor counter is not evidence because it increments on every image load including bots and repeat loads, and public scripts inflate it
Identifies the audience mismatch: these widgets read as engagement to an early-career peer group and as noise to the senior technical reviewer being targeted
States that the widgets cannot see private work at all
Prescribes the fix as pinned original repositories with descriptions and outcome lines plus the anonymized private-contribution toggle, not merely fewer widgets
Flags 'Full-stack developer passionate about clean code' as absent or vague positioning
Requires one sentence of prose above every image, badge and widget
Requires alt text on every retained visual element, no meaning encoded in colour alone, and readability in a plain markdown viewer

evals.prompt: I'm giving a talk at a regional Go conference on 3 November, and today is 20 October. My profile is a mess. I can find maybe four hours total before then, and honestly after the talk nobody is going to look at this file again. I'm the only person with access to my account and I know I won't remember to revisit it. Right now the profile says I'm 'currently building' a scheduler I archived last year, the banner image is broken so the README shows nothing, pins are unset, and there's no real intro line. What order do I do things in? Handle is renske-boomgaard.
evals.expected_output: Three stated orderings that disagree, led by the efficiency one, with the false claim and the render repair tied at the top, the page rebuild dropped because of the date, and the review habit deleted because there is no standing owner.
expectations: States the fix ordering out loud rather than implying it by row order
Emits at least three separate orderings - by effort, by value and by efficiency - and notes that they disagree
Leads with the efficiency ordering
Places killing the false claim and repairing the render tied at the top, explaining they tie because each takes minutes and each fixes a page that is wrong rather than merely weak
Puts removing or updating the archived 'currently building' scheduler line first or tied first
Puts repairing the broken render first or tied first
Places setting the six pins ahead of the positioning sentence on the efficiency ordering
Drops the full page rebuild from this pass because of the 3 November date
Deletes the review habit from the plan outright rather than listing it last, because there is no standing owner
Names which of the user's answers moved which fix in the presented plan
Keeps the recommended work inside the stated four-hour ceiling
Replaces the undated 'currently building' line with a dated line or deletes it, rather than rewriting it as another undated claim

evals.prompt:
Audit this for me. It is the whole profile README for the account halvard-nyqvist:

# Hey there 👋
![banner](banner.png)
Software engineer. I love building things and learning new technologies.
🔭 I'm currently working on something exciting
🌱 Learning Rust
📫 Reach me: halvard@nyqvist.dev
[my blog](https://blog.nyqvist.dev)

Pins are whatever GitHub picked for me. Just tell me if it is good enough to leave alone.
evals.expected_output: A scored audit in the skill's report format - four blocking checks, eight scored checks out of 16, a cold-reader line and a fix order - with evidence quoted per line, the self-set nature of the thresholds stated once, and agreement sought before any rewrite.
expectations: Produces the report in the scorecard format: blocking checks, then scored checks, then cold reader, then fix order
Reports exactly four blocking checks
Reports eight scored checks worth two points each, for a total out of 16
Attaches evidence to each scored line - a quoted sentence, a field value, or a line of audit output
Fails or flags the undated "I'm currently working on something exciting" line under the claims-are-true blocking check
Scores the positioning check at or near zero and quotes 'I love building things and learning new technologies' as the evidence
Flags that pins are unset and that the fallback 'Popular repositories' ordering is not controlled by the owner
States the ship bar as 13 of 16 with all four blocking checks passing
States explicitly that the checks and the pass mark are this skill's own baseline rather than a published or industry standard
Describes the cold-reader test as 45 seconds on the page followed by four questions, with four of four as the pass
States that the auditor's own reading does not count as the cold reader, and offers a person or a fresh session with no context on the account instead
Presents the score and seeks the owner's agreement before rewriting anything

evals.prompt: I maintain 31 public repos. My goal for the profile is getting more people to actually contribute, because I'm drowning in issues and nobody is helping. I was going to pin my top six by stars: an awesome-links list (4.1k), an old dotfiles repo (900), a fork of someone's CLI where I fixed a typo (700, because the upstream is popular), my main library gsdcache (610), an archived experiment (380), and a conference demo (120). Sound right? Account is wren-adeyemi.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the star-ranked selection, a pin set chosen against the stated contributors goal with an explicit internal order, and named exclusions for the archived repository and the trivially modified fork.
expectations: Rejects ordering pins by star count
States that the platform already displays star counts, so star-ranked pins repeat information the visitor can already see
Selects the contributors pin set because the stated goal is contributors
Orders that set as the repository with curated good-first-issues first, then the one with the best contributor documentation
Rejects pinning the archived experiment
Rejects pinning the fork that was not substantially changed
States that leaving pins unset is worse than an imperfect set, because the platform falls back to auto-selected 'Popular repositories'
Requires each pinned repository to have a description and topics before it is pinned
States that a bare pin wastes one of only six slots
States that a personal account has six pin slots, repositories and gists combined
Declines to rank the four pin sets against each other, on the grounds that the goal answer selects one outright and every pin costs the same to set
Confirms that the order within the chosen set is real because it decides which repository a visitor opens first

evals.prompt: We shipped the new org profile for Quillmark on 1 September. My VP wants a number by the end of the quarter proving it worked. I've added a visitor-counter badge to the README and it's already at 4,200, which seems great, and separately I'm tracking our star count week over week: we went from 2,810 to 3,050 since the rewrite. Is that enough to show, or should I add something else?
evals.expected_output: Both proposed numbers deleted from the plan with reasons, replaced by a three-item measurement order led by tagged click-through, with qualified inbound promoted because this is an organization.
expectations: Deletes the visitor-counter badge from the measurement plan rather than ranking it last
Explains that the counter increments on every image load through an anonymizing proxy, counting bots and repeat loads, and that public scripts inflate it
Deletes star growth from the measurement plan rather than ranking it last
States that star growth after a profile change is unattributable and that stars follow promotion rather than the page
Declines to credit the move from 2,810 to 3,050 stars to the profile rewrite
Names tagged click-through to an owner-controlled destination as the first thing to build, costing roughly an hour, with the destination's analytics belonging to the owner
Names pinned-repository traffic second and states it is limited to a trailing 14-day window
States that pinned-repository traffic requires push access to that specific repository
Names qualified inbound as what the efficiency order starves, and promotes it here because the account is an organization
Defines qualified inbound for an organization as a prospect who already knows what the company builds instead of asking
States that no host offers profile-level analytics, and that the ship date must be written down with confounders annotated

evals.prompt: Working on the profile for my project Tideglass, a schema-diffing tool for Postgres migrations. About half my users are solo devs who just install it and run it, and half are platform teams at banks who need to know it won't disappear on them. Give me a good one-liner for the top of my account page and I'll take it from there. My handle is bea-okonkwo.
evals.expected_output: Three positioning candidates on different axes with trade-offs and a recommendation, plus a structure that serves both adoption motions from one first screen with a lower evaluation block.
expectations: Produces three candidate positioning sentences rather than one
Builds the three candidates on different axes: what is built mechanically, what problem is removed for the reader, and what the reader can stop doing
States the trade-off of each candidate, gives an explicit recommendation, and leaves the choice to the owner
Applies the test that a competitor's account must not be able to paste the sentence unchanged
States that the sentence propagates into the bio, the organization tagline, link unfurls and search listings
Identifies that both adoption motions are in play and does not force a choice between them
States the solo developer's dominant question as whether this person can build the thing they need
States the team's dominant question as what they are depending on and who answers when it breaks
Names licensing stance, maintenance cadence, and support or security routes as what must surface early for the team audience
Names the absence of an answer to 'who maintains this' as the fatal omission for the team audience
Keeps the first screen identical for both audiences and adds a short evaluation block lower down rather than writing the top twice
Recommends a plain-language project status line such as maintained, seeking maintainers, or feature-frozen

evals.prompt: We moved everything off GitHub to a self-hosted Forgejo instance 18 months ago and our org page there is embarrassing. Is there a proper framework for this kind of thing, something with a name I can put in a deck for our engineering leadership? Company is Kestrel Freight Systems, about 60 engineers, we open-source two Rust crates and keep the rest internal.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to supply or invent a named framework, the audience question plus the scorecard offered instead, and an explicit statement that the bundled audit script is GitHub-only so the checklist must be applied by hand.
expectations: States that no validated framework exists for profile work
Declines to name or repeat the one coined acronym framework in circulation, noting it has no adoption beyond its own post
Declines to invent a replacement framework or acronym for the deck
Offers the audience question plus the scorecard as what does the work a framework would claim to do
States that the bundled audit script calls GitHub's own APIs and has no equivalent for a self-hosted forge
Directs applying the same checklist by hand from the profile page itself
States plainly which facts could not be verified rather than assuming them
Notes that other forges expose different profile surfaces, so pin counts and contribution-graph mechanics do not transfer unchanged
Asks whether this is the organization page or a personal profile, and what one outcome the page should produce, before proposing content
Requires the open-source stance to state which two crates are open and that the rest is internal
States that the scorecard thresholds are self-set defaults the owner can move with a reason

evals.prompt: Board meeting in three weeks. One of our investors keeps comparing our 1,900 stars to a competitor's 14,000 and asking why the gap. Our head of growth found a service that will deliver 5,000 stars for about the price of one conference booth, and separately suggested we run a 'star us' banner on the org profile and in our CLI output. We're Halverd Systems, 22 people, our core engine is Apache-2.0. What should I do?
evals.expected_output: A named refusal of the star purchase backed by the fake-star study, the option deleted from the plan rather than ranked last, and a redirect to adoption evidence the organization profile can honestly carry.
expectations: Refuses buying stars by name and states the practice is detectable
Cites roughly six million suspected fake stars across more than eighteen thousand repositories, from a multi-year study of public event data
Deletes the star-buying option from the plan rather than ranking it last
States that stars measure attention and promotion reach, not adoption or quality
States that star growth is driven by promotion rather than by the profile page
Recommends contextualizing stars next to adoption data when investors ask, rather than optimizing stars
Names concrete adoption evidence to publish instead: named users, download counts, and release cadence
Declines to treat the 1,900 versus 14,000 comparison as a measure of relative adoption or quality
Identifies the request as one to manufacture evidence, says so plainly, and offers the profile audit instead
Does not promise that any profile change will close the star gap
Recommends the organization README state the open-source stance, including that the core engine is Apache-2.0 and what is commercial
